Who Is Jes Us? 39  
with the risen Jesus Christ. Over the years I have also experienced 
that Jesus Christ is alive today. I have experienced his love, his 
power and the reality of a relationship that convinces me that he 
really is alive. As the fictional character Sherlock Holmes said, ‘When 
you have eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however 
improbable, must be the truth.’14
We saw, when we looked earlier in the chapter at what Jesus said 
about himself, that there were only three realistic possibilities – 
either he was and is the Son of God, or else deluded or something 
more sinister. When one looks at the evidence it does not make sense 
to say that he was insane or evil. The whole weight of his teaching, his 
works, his character, his fulfilment of Old Testament prophecy and 
his conquest of death make those suggestions absurd, illogical and 
unbelievable. On the other hand, they lend the strongest possible 
support to Jesus’ own self-understanding as a man whose identity 
was God.
In conclusion, as C. S. Lewis pointed out: ‘We are faced, then, 
with a frightening alternative.’15 Either Jesus was (and is) exactly what 
he said, or else he was insane or something worse. To C. S. Lewis it 
seemed clear that he could have been neither insane nor evil, and 
thus he concludes, ‘however strange or terrifying or unlikely it may 
seem, I have to accept the view that He was and is God.’16
